## TL;DR

Round three closed two review findings against the automatic worktree GC. First,
`git status` hides ignored files, so a resolved worktree holding only a local
`.env` or `work/.attachments/` looked clean and was force-removed; the sweep now
inspects ignored paths and keeps anything that is not provably regenerable (or
an inherited symlink into the canonical checkout). Second, retained worktrees
were reported before their commits, changed source paths, and dirty paths were
measured; retention is now an audit as well as a decision, with structured
fields mirrored by `repoos status` and `repoos gc --dry-run`.

## Work and rationale

The force-removal path is the dangerous one. `repoos/integrate/*` candidates are
throwaway, but a candidate can still hold a local secret or test attachment, and
a resolved feature worktree can hold one while being byte-identical to main in
every tracked path. Both are now checked with `git status --ignored=matching`.
Only known build/install output (`dist/`, `node_modules/`, `coverage/`,
`.repoos/`, VitePress cache) is treated as disposable. Any other ignored path
keeps the worktree with an `ignored files may hold local data` reason.

The one deliberate exception is an ignored `.env` symlink whose target resolves
inside the canonical main checkout. `ensureWorktree` links `.env` that way, and
removing the link leaves the secret in place, so failing closed there would
block cleanup of every normal worktree for no safety gain. A real `.env` file
still keeps the worktree, as do `.env*.local`, attachment trees, and scratch
directories.

For the audit gap, I moved detail collection ahead of the lifecycle verdict.
Every retained entry now carries `commitsAhead`, `changedSourcePaths` (all
non-task paths the branch changed relative to its merge base with main),
`dirtyPaths`, and `ignoredPaths`. This includes active, review, and
human-assigned worktrees, which previously returned before any measurement.
The five-path reason string remains a summary; the structured array is the
record. `repoos status` mirrors the fields, and `repoos gc` prints a compact
detail line under each retained entry so an operator can see what is inside
without rerunning the sweep.

## Approaches tried

I first considered treating every ignored path as unsafe. That is simple, but it
would retain every worktree with an inherited `.env` symlink or a rebuilt
`dist/`, which is effectively every worktree the pipeline touches. The
allowlist plus the symlink-target check keeps the fail-closed property while
still allowing cleanup where the data is provably regenerable or stored
elsewhere.

I also considered folding ignored paths into `dirtyPaths`. Keeping them separate
is clearer: normal dirt drives the "task-file-only" rule, while ignored data is
an independent safety gate that must be answered before any force removal.

## Challenges and blockers

The fixes landed but the turn crashed before handoff. This recovery pass re-ran
the targeted GC and status suites (65 tests) and `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main
repoos check` on the clean tree, both green, so the branch is ready to hand off
without further code changes.

The main subtlety was distinguishing a real ignored `.env` from the inherited
symlink. `lstatSync` plus a realpath containment check handles it; a dangling
symlink is safe because no data is reachable. The test suite covers both cases,
including a probe that the canonical `.env` survives removal.

Another subtlety was measurement cost: `changedSourcePaths` needs a merge-base
and a diff per retained worktree, not just the cheap ancestry check. Restricting
that work to retained entries keeps the sweep proportional to what is actually
reported, and the diff is chunk-free because it is one invocation.

The scoped check's remote validation was unavailable this round: the runner
container hung on one host and the two retry hosts failed, so the check aborted
without a verdict. I re-ran the same changed-path check with `--local-tests`,
which exercises the scoped suite locally instead of skipping it for the remote
runner. That is an environment failure, not a code failure.

## Key learnings

`git status --porcelain` is a poor "is this worktree safe to delete" oracle when
the repo ignores secrets and attachments: it answers "what would I commit",
not "what would I lose". Any force-removal path needs an explicit ignored-data
pass. Separately, a report that decides first and measures later cannot satisfy
an audit requirement, even when its reasons are correct — the decision and the
evidence have to be collected together.
